candidate_relations.reason: A circumscribed paraspinal retroperitoneal mass can mimic sarcoma radiographically, but the reference identifies a benign nerve-sheath tumor rather than sarcoma.
The solitary 5 cm well-circumscribed lesion is unlike the plaque-like infiltrative tissue that characterizes retroperitoneal fibrosis.
Normal chest and brain staging and a single sharply marginated mass do not provide evidence for lymphoma over the stated schwannoma.
The patient had unremarkable laboratory studies and no fever, while imaging showed a solid heterogeneously enhancing mass rather than a fluid collection.
No nodal disease or systemic findings accompany the isolated iliopsoas-adjacent lesion, making retroperitoneal lymphoma a separate diagnosis.
Neuroblastoma is an incompatible tumor type in this 36-year-old with a localized, slowly symptomatic retroperitoneal mass.
The candidate names the same schwannoma represented by the well-circumscribed T1-low, T2-high retroperitoneal lesion selected for core biopsy.
The CT description contains heterogeneous enhancement but no macroscopic fat or adipocytic features to support liposarcoma.
FDG avidity of 5.2 is nonspecific and does not convert the stated schwannoma into a solitary fibrous tumor.
No fat, calcification, cystic components, or other mixed-tissue CT features of a retroperitoneal teratoma are reported.
Chest and brain CT were normal and there is no known primary cancer to support a retroperitoneal metastasis.
Although both are nerve-sheath tumors, the circumscribed lesion and reference diagnosis do not support the malignant peripheral nerve sheath subtype.
The paraspinal location is compatible with a neurogenic tumor, but that family label omits the required schwannoma histotype.
The localized, well-demarcated mass is designated schwannoma and the record supplies no malignant histology establishing a sarcoma.
